PART I Foundations What a database is, how to model data, how to normalise it, and where the bytes actually live. What a Database Is Data Modeling Normalization and Denormalization Storage Types

CHAPTER 01 What a Database Is An organised collection of structured data, stored electronically and accessed by applications, so that data can be stored, retrieved, updated and deleted efficiently. K E Y TA K E AWAY. Good database design ensures data integrity, high performance and scalability. TWO FAMILIES SQL (RELATIONAL) NOSQL (NON-RELATIONAL) Model Tables, rows, columns, fixed schema Document, key-value, wide-column, graph Examples MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Neo4j Strength Joins, constraints, ACID transactions Flexible schema, horizontal scale, specialised access patterns RDBMS VOCABULARY TERM MEANING Table A collection of rows with the same shape Row (tuple, record) One entry in the table Column (attribute, field) One named property of every row Primary key Uniquely identifies a row; unique and not null Foreign key A column that references the primary key of another table Constraint A rule the database enforces on the data Index An auxiliary structure that speeds up lookups CONSTRAINTS CONSTRAINT GUARANTEES NOT NULL The column cannot be null UNIQUE All values in the column are distinct PRIMARY KEY Unique and not null FOREIGN KEY Referential integrity between tables CHECK A condition holds for every row DEFAULT A value is supplied when none is given

WHAT A DATABASE IS COMMON COMMANDS SHOW DATABASES; USE shop; DESC orders; SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10; EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders; DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 1; R E M E M B E R . Constraints are the cheapest bug prevention you have: the database rejects bad data even when the application forgets to.

CHAPTER 02 Data Modeling The blueprint of your data. Good models make systems easier to build, scale and maintain. Data modeling is the process of defining structure, relationships and rules for data in a system. Its goals: organise data logically, reduce redundancy, ensure integrity, support queries and performance, and adapt to change. THREE LEVELS OF MODEL LEVEL DESCRIBES EXAMPLE Conceptual High-level entities and relationships ER diagram Logical Detailed structure, independent of the engine Tables, keys, attributes Physical Implementation specifics Types, indexes, partitions Other model families: dimensional, object, graph, document, key‐value. THE MODELING PROCESS Understand the business Identify entities Define attributes Define relationships → → → Define constraints Validate and refine → → Understand the business. Gather requirements and data sources. Identify entities. Find the key data objects (customer, order, product). Define attributes. The properties of each entity. Define relationships. Associations and cardinality. Define constraints and rules. Keys, business rules, validation. Validate and refine. Review, normalise, optimise. KEY CONCEPTS Entity: a distinguishable object or concept. Attribute: a property or characteristic of an entity. Relationship: an association between entities.

DATA MODELING Cardinality: how many instances take part in a relationship. CARDINALIT Y MEANING EXAMPLE 1:1 One to one User and profile 1:N One to many Customer and orders N:1 Many to one Orders and customer M:N Many to many Students and courses (needs a join table) K E Y S KEY MEANING Primary key Uniquely identifies a record Candidate key A minimal set of attributes that could be the primary key Foreign key References the primary key in another table Composite key A primary key made of several attributes EXAMPLE: E-COMMERCE MODEL CUSTOMER 1---N ORDER ORDER 1---N ORDER_ITEM PRODUCT 1---N ORDER_ITEM ORDER 1---1 PAYMENT CUSTOMER 1---N ADDRESS CATEGORY 1---N PRODUCT (self-reference via parent_category_id) LOGICAL SCHEMA CREATE TABLE customers ( customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL, phone VARCHAR(20), created_at DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); CREATE TABLE orders ( order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL, order_date DATETIME NOT NULL, status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, total_amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id) );

COMMON DATA TYPES T YPE USE INT / BIGINT Integer numbers DECIMAL(p,s) Exact numeric; use for money VARCHAR(n) Variable-length string TEXT Long text DATE , DATETIME Date, date and time BOOLEAN True or false JSON JSON document UUID Universally unique identifier DIMENSIONAL MODELING (ANALYTICS) A star schema puts a central fact table (measurable events, numeric) in the middle and surrounds it with dimension tables that provide context: date, product, store, customer. It is simple and fast for reporting queries. MODELING CHECKLIST All required entities and attributes captured Primary keys defined for every entity Relationships and cardinalities correct Constraints (PK, FK, unique, not null) defined Normalised appropriately Indexes planned for performance Data growth and change considered Model aligned with business rules and validated with stakeholders COMMON PITFALLS Over‐normalisation hurts performance. Under‐normalisation causes redundancy. Missing constraints let bad data in. Wrong data types waste space and break com‐ parisons. Ignoring future scale and having no indexing strategy both surface late and cost most. Not involving stakeholders produces a clean model of the wrong thing. R E M E M B E R . Good data models make systems easier to build, scale and main‐ tain.

NORMALIZATION AND DENORMALIZATION CHAPTER 03 Normalization and Denormalization Normalization minimises redundancy and avoids update, insert and delete anomalies. Each form builds on the previous one. 1NF → 2NF → 3NF → BCNF FORM RULE 1NF Atomic values, no repeating groups, each column holds a single value, rows are unique 2NF In 1NF, and no partial dependency: no non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key 3NF In 2NF, and no transitive dependency: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute BCNF A stronger 3NF: every determinant is a candidate key BAD DESIGN VERSUS GOOD DESIGN A single orders table that repeats user_name , user_email and user_phone on every row stores the same user data many times. Change an email and you must change every row; miss one and the data is inconsistent. The fix: a users table ( id , name , email , created_at ) and an orders table that holds only user_id as a foreign key plus order-specific columns. DENORMALIZATION: WHEN AND HOW Denormalise deliberately, once you have measured a problem. WHEN HOW Read performance is critical Add redundant data Complex joins hurt performance Pre-compute aggregates The data is relatively stable Use materialised views Example: instead of summing order_items every time you show an order, store total_amount on orders . You balance write cost (keep it in sync) against read cost. R E M E M B E R . Normalise first for correctness; denormalise selectively for read speed. Never the other way round.

CHAPTER 05 SQL in an RDBMS SQL commands fall into five families. Know which family a command belongs to and you can answer most "what does it do" questions. DDL → DML → DQL → DCL → TCL FAMILY FULL NAME THINK COMMANDS DDL Data Definition Language Structure CREATE , ALTER , DROP , TRUNCATE , RENAME DML Data Manipulation Language Data INSERT , UPDATE , DELETE DQL Data Query Language Query SELECT DCL Data Control Language Access GRANT , REVOKE TCL Transaction Control Language Transactions COMMIT , ROLLBACK , SAVEPOINT SELECT is sometimes grouped under DML, but strictly it is DQL. DDL: STRUCTURE CREATE TABLE employee ( id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), salary DECIMAL(10,2) ); ALTER TABLE employee ADD department VARCHAR(50); TRUNCATE TABLE employee; DROP TABLE employee; COMMAND PURPOSE CREATE Create a new object (database, table, index) ALTER Change the structure of an existing object DROP Delete an object entirely TRUNCATE Remove all rows but keep the structure RENAME Rename an object DDL changes auto-commit in most DBMS.

SQL IN AN RDBMS DML: DATA INSERT INTO employee (id, name, salary) VALUES (1, 'Nitesh', 100000); UPDATE employee SET salary = 120000 WHERE id = 1; DELETE FROM employee WHERE id = 1; DQL: QUERY SELECT id, name, salary, department FROM employee WHERE salary > 100000 ORDER BY salary DESC; DCL: ACCESS GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON employee TO user1; REVOKE INSERT ON employee FROM user1; TCL: TRANSACTIONS START TRANSACTION; UPDATE employee SET salary = 150000 WHERE id = 1; SAVEPOINT salary_update; UPDATE employee SET salary = 200000 WHERE id = 1; ROLLBACK TO salary_update; COMMIT; Flow: start, update, savepoint, update, rollback to savepoint, commit. Only the first update survives. CLASSIC COMPARISON: DELETE, TRUNCATE, DROP DELETE TRUNCATE D R O P Family DML DDL DDL Removes Selected rows (with WHERE ) All rows Rows and the table itself Rollback Yes, inside a transaction Generally no (engine- dependent) Generally no Speed Slower, row by row Fast Fast EASY MNEMONIC DDL defines the structure. DML manipulates the data. DQL queries the data. DCL controls access. TCL controls transactions. R E M E M B E R . DDL changes auto‐commit in most DBMS. DML changes are con‐ trolled by TCL. Always commit important transactions, and use DCL for secur‐ ity.

CHAPTER 06 SQL Cheat Sheet From basic to advanced, on one page of reading. BASICS AND FILTERING SELECT column(s) FROM table WHERE condition; SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 18 AND city = 'Delhi'; CONDITION MEANING = , -= Equal, not equal > , < , -= , -= Comparisons AND Both conditions true OR Either condition true NOT Negates the condition SORTING AND LIMITING SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5; AGGREGATE FUNCTIONS FUNCTION RESULT COUNT() Number of rows SUM() Total AVG() Average MIN() , MAX() Smallest, largest value GROUP BY AND HAVING SELECT column, COUNT(*) FROM table GROUP BY column HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; GROUP BY groups rows with the same values. HAVING filters on the aggregated result; WHERE filters rows before grouping. TABLE OPERATIONS CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50), age INT); ALTER TABLE users ADD email VARCHAR(100); DROP TABLE users;

SQL CHEAT SHEET SUBQUERIES SELECT name FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders); INDEXES AND VIEWS CREATE INDEX idx_name ON users(name); -- speeds up queries CREATE VIEW user_view AS SELECT name, age FROM users; -- virtual table ADVANCED CONCEPTS Window function: a calculation across a set of related rows without collapsing them. SELECT name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM employees; CTE (common table expression): makes complex queries easier to read and reuse. WITH adults AS ( SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 18 ) SELECT * FROM adults; CASE: conditional logic in a query. SELECT name, CASE WHEN age > 18 THEN 'Adult' ELSE 'Minor' END AS category FROM users; SET OPERATIONS AND DATA TYPES OPERATION BEHAVIOUR UNION Combine results, remove duplicates UNION ALL Combine results, keep duplicates (faster) INTERSECT Rows common to both EXCEPT / MINUS Rows in the first but not the second Useful types: INT , VARCHAR(n) , CHAR(n) (fixed length), DATE / DATETIME , DECIMAL(p,s) . USEFUL HABITS Back up data regularly. Follow naming conventions. Test queries on sample data. Validate in production before you trust a query. REMEMBER. WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups. UNION ALL when you know there are no duplicates.

CHAPTER 07 SQL Joins Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. Assume two tables. A (Employees): (1, John, 10), (2, Mary, 20), (3, Mike, 30), (4, Sara, 40). B (Departments): (10, HR), (20, IT), (30, Finance), (50, Sales). They match on DeptID ; Sara's de‐ partment 40 has no match in B, and department 50 has no employee in A. THE JOIN TYPES JOIN RETURNS IN THE EXAMPLE INNER JOIN Only rows matching in both tables John, Mary, Mike LEFT (OUTER) All rows from A, matching rows from B, NULL when Adds Sara with NULL JOIN no match department RIGHT (OUTER) All rows from B, matching rows from A, NULL when Adds Sales with NULL JOIN no match employee FULL (OUTER) All rows from both, NULL on the non-matching side Sara and Sales both appear JOIN CROSS JOIN Cartesian product, rows in A × rows in B 4 × 4 = 16 rows SELF JOIN A table joined with itself Employee and manager SYNTAX SELECT * FROM A INNER JOIN B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; SELECT * FROM A RIGHT JOIN B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; SELECT * FROM A FULL OUTER JOIN B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; SELECT * FROM A CROSS JOIN B; -- Self join: employee and manager SELECT e1.Name AS Employee, e2.Name AS Manager FROM Employees e1 LEFT JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.ManagerID = e2.ID; MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN ; emulate it with LEFT JOIN --. UNION --. RIGHT JOIN . WHICH ONE TO USE INNER: you need only related data. LEFT: keep all records from the left table, with or without a match. RIGHT: keep all records from the right table. FULL OUTER: you need all data from both tables. CROSS: rarely needed in real scenarios. Be sure you meant it. R E M E M B E R . A filter on the right table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join. Put such conditions in the ON clause to keep the unmatched left rows.

SQL QUERY EXECUTION ORDER CHAPTER 08 SQL Query Execution Order SQL is declarative, but the database processes the query in a specific logical order. You write SELECT first; the engine reaches it sixth. SELECT e.name, d.department_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id WHERE e.status = 'Active' GROUP BY d.department_name HAVING COUNT(e.id) > 5 ORDER BY d.department_name LIMIT 10; FROM → JOIN WHERE GROUP BY HAVING SELECT → → → → ORDER BY LIMIT / OFFSET → → # CLAUSE WHAT HAPPENS 1 FROM Identify the tables or data sources 2 JOIN Combine rows from multiple tables 3 WHERE Filter rows on the specified conditions 4 GROUP BY Group rows by the specified column(s) 5 HAVING Filter groups on aggregated data 6 SELECT Choose the columns and expressions to return 7 ORDER BY Sort the result set 8 LIMIT / OFFSET Limit rows returned, or skip rows WHY IT MATTERS You cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE or HAVING in standard SQL, because SELECT has not run yet. ORDER BY can use it, because it runs after. WHERE cannot contain aggregates; the groups do not exist yet. Use HAVING . DISTINCT is applied after SELECT , before ORDER BY . R E M E M B E R . While SQL lets you write clauses in a fixed order, the database fol‐ lows this logical execution order to produce the final result.

CHAPTER 09 How a Query Runs Inside the Database From the string you send to the rows you get back, a query passes through ten stages. SQL query → Parser Query tree Optimizer Execution plan → → → Index scan? Find data Read pages Return rows → → → → THE STAGES SQL query. The user writes a query, for example SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = 10 AND salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC; . Parser. Checks syntax, validates table and column names, checks permissions, and produces an internal representation. Query tree. The parser builds a tree of the logical structure. Nodes are operations: SELECT (projection), FILTER (conditions), SORT (ordering), TABLE (data source). 3. Optimizer / planner. Evaluates alternative execution strategies using statistics and metadata (table size, indexes, data distribution). It is cost-based : it compares plans, estimates cost (I/O, CPU, memory) and picks the cheapest. Execution plan. The chosen sequence of operations, with access methods, estimated cost and expected rows. Example: index scan on department_id , filter salary > 50000 , sort by salary DESC , return result. Index scan? The engine checks whether a usable index exists. If yes, perform an index scan (faster): skip non-matching rows, jump directly to matches, reduce I/O. If no, do a full table scan (slower). Find matching data. Using the index or table scan, the engine locates row pointers (RID or primary key) and applies all conditions, keeping only qualifying rows. Read required pages. Data pages come from disk or, preferably, the buffer cache. Reading fewer pages means better performance. Return rows. The final result set goes back to the client in the requested format. R E M E M B E R . You describe what you want; the optimizer decides how to get it. Your job is to give it good schema, good indexes and fresh statistics. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. WHAT TO REMEMBER ABOUT THE OPTIMIZER The optimizer is only as good as its statistics. Stale statistics produce bad plans (see the indexing-failure chapter). EXPLAIN shows the plan it chose.

CHAPTER 10 How Database Indexing Works Indexes are special data structures that help the database find data quickly without scanning the entire table. A N A LO GY. An index is like the index of a book: it helps you find what you need without reading the whole book. WHY INDEX Speeds up data retrieval and avoids full table scans. Improves ORDER BY , GROUP BY and DISTINCT performance. Enforces uniqueness (unique index) and supports efficient joins. COST Without an index O(N), a full table scan reading every row With an index O(log N), a fast lookup THE STRUCTURE: B+ TREE Most databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server) use a B+ tree for indexes. A balanced tree, so search is always O(log N). Internal nodes hold keys that guide the search. Leaf nodes hold the actual data pointers (row IDs), or the rows themselves in a clustered index. Leaves are linked , which makes range scans fast. A QUERY WITH AND WITHOUT AN INDEX SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = 'Delhi'; WITHOUT AN INDEX WITH AN INDEX ON C I T Y Scan every row one by one and compare Walk the tree to Delhi , get row IDs (1, 3, 5, ...) Cost O(N) Fetch exactly those rows, return to the client

HOW DATABASE INDEXING WORKS WITHOUT AN INDEX WITH AN INDEX ON C I T Y Cost O(log N), far fewer disk I/Os TYPES OF INDEXES T YPE NOTES Primary Created automatically on the primary key; unique and not null Secondary On non-primary-key columns to speed up searches there Unique Ensures all values are unique (some DBs allow one NULL) Composite (multi-column) Order of columns matters: an index on (a, b) serves a, or a and b Full-text Text search ( MATCH --. AGAINST in MySQL) Spatial Geographic data (GIS) Other physical kinds you will meet: hash (fast equality lookup) and covering in‐ dexes. WHEN AN INDEX IS USED, AND WHEN NOT USED NOT USED WHERE (equality or range) Functions on the indexed column, WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ALICE' JOIN conditions Leading wildcard, LIKE '%abc' ORDER BY , GROUP BY , DISTINCT OR across different columns Low-selectivity columns (gender, flags) The query optimizer decides whether to use an index. It is a cost decision, not a rule. INDEX VERSUS FULL TABLE SCAN SCENARIO INDEX FULL SCAN Few rows match Faster Slower Many rows match Slower Faster Small table Overhead Faster Large table Much faster Very slow TRADE-OFFS Extra storage: indexes take disk space. Slower writes: INSERT , UPDATE and DELETE must also update the index.

Maintenance overhead: more indexes, more overhead. Too many hurt perform‐ ance. BEST PRACTICES Index columns used in WHERE , JOIN , ORDER BY , GROUP BY . Use composite indexes wisely: put the most selective column first, but also match your query patterns. Avoid indexing low‐cardinality columns. Do not over‐index. Regularly review and remove unused indexes. Use EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to verify usage. READING EXPLAIN (MYSQL) EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = 'Delhi'; -- type: ref -> an index lookup was used -- key: idx_city -> which index -- rows: 5 -> estimated rows scanned (lower is better) HOW TO ANSWER IN AN INTERVIEW Explain what an index is and why it is needed. Explain the underlying structure (B+ tree). Walk through query execution with and without an index. Name the index types with examples. Discuss when it is used and not used. Mention trade‐offs. Al‐ ways mention the query optimizer's role. Use a diagram if you can. R E M E M B E R . Good indexing means faster queries and happy users.

CLUSTERED VS NON-CLUSTERED INDEX CHAPTER 11 Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index Both improve retrieval speed. They differ in where the data physically lives. CLUSTERED NON-CLUSTERED Data layout Rows are physically stored in index order Index structure is separate from the table data Leaf nodes Contain the actual data rows Contain pointers (row ID or primary key) How many Only one per table Many per table Lookup Root, leaf, data row (very fast) Index search, find pointer, table access path (more steps) Range Very efficient: seek, then scan Less efficient: pointer lookups then table queries sequentially access Write cost Inserts and updates may cause page splits Extra overhead on every write CLUSTERED INDEX EXAMPLE An Employee table clustered on id is stored on disk in id order. A B+ tree sits over it: the root routes to internal nodes, and the leaves are the rows ( 1 Alice, 2 Bob ; 4 David, 5 Emma ), linked in order. SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE id = 3; -- Root -> Leaf -> Data row (very fast) NON-CLUSTERED INDEX EXAMPLE The table (heap) holds rows in no particular order, each with a row ID. A separate B+ tree on name stores Alice -> 101 , Bob -> 102 , and so on. SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE name = 'Charlie'; -- Index search -> find pointer -> table access -> data row (more steps)

RANGE QUERY PERFORMANCE For a range like id BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000 , a clustered index seeks to 1000 and scans sequentially to 2000. A non‐clustered index seeks, then does a pointer lookup and table access per row, which is less efficient. COVERING INDEX A non‐clustered index that contains every column a query needs, so the table is never touched. CREATE INDEX idx_user ON Users(email) INCLUDE (name, city); -- A query on email, name, city is answered from the index alone. INCLUDE is supported in SQL Server and PostgreSQL 11+; in MySQL, add the columns to the index key instead. WHEN TO USE WHICH CLUSTERED, USE FOR NON-CLUSTERED, USE FOR Primary key Search columns Range queries WHERE conditions Sequential reads JOIN columns Frequently queried fields Covering indexes Time-series data Email, phone, username, status, department ID Typical clustered keys: OrderID , UserID , CreatedAt , TransactionID . MEMORY TRICK A clustered index is the book content : the actual pages in order. A non‐clustered in‐ dex is the book index page : keyword to page number. R E M E M B E R . Most databases use the primary key as the clustered index by de‐ fault (implementation varies; in MySQL InnoDB it always does). Additional searchable columns are typically indexed with non‐clustered indexes.

WHEN INDEXING FAILS CHAPTER 12 When Indexing Fails Indexes are powerful, but not magic. They do not help when the query or the data prevents their use. Nine classic reasons. FUNCTIONS ON THE INDEXED COLUMN Wrapping the column in UPPER() , DATE() , SUBSTR() forces the database to compute the function for every row, so the index cannot be used. -- Bad WHERE UPPER(name) = 'JOHN' -- Better WHERE name = 'John' Where you genuinely need the function, create a functional (expression) index on it. TYPE MISMATCH Comparing different data types forces implicit conversions and can force a full scan. WHERE id = '123' -- id is INT: implicit conversion may kill index usage LEADING WILDCARD IN LIKE LIKE '%abc' cannot use the index because the start of the string is unknown. WHERE name LIKE '%abc' -- full scan WHERE name LIKE 'abc%' -- can use the index OR CONDITIONS ON DIFFERENT COLUMNS WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2 often prevents index usage and the optimizer may choose a full table scan. Rewrite as a UNION of two indexed queries, or index both columns so the engine can combine them.

NOT EQUAL / NOT IN -> , NOT IN and -= have low selectivity and are usually inefficient for indexes. The database may prefer a full scan. LOW SELECTIVITY When 90% of rows are ACTIVE , an index on status is not selective, and the data‐ base rightly prefers scanning over index lookups. COMPOSITE INDEX RULE VIOLATION An index on (A, B, C) works only if queries use the leftmost columns. WHERE b = 1 -- skips A: index not usable WHERE a = 1 AND b = 1 -- usable WRAPPING IN A SUBQUERY OR VIEW The optimizer may not push predicates down, leading to full scans. WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM t WHERE status = 'A') OUTDATED STATISTICS Poor or outdated statistics mislead the optimizer: a wrong plan is chosen and the index is ignored. Typical cause: a table updated heavily after a bulk insert or up‐ date. Refresh with ANALYZE . BONUS Sometimes the query is just not selective enough, or the table is too small for an in‐ dex to matter. R E M E M B E R . Indexes help the right query. Write SQL the optimizer can love. Good schema + good data + good SQL = happy indexes. Measure, analyse, op‐ timise, repeat.

PAGING AND FRAGMENTATION CHAPTER 13 Paging and Fragmentation Data in databases is stored on disk in fixed-size blocks called pages . Over time, pages can become fragmented. WHAT IS A PAGE The smallest unit of I/O between disk and memory. Typical sizes are 4 KB, 8 KB, 16 KB or 32 KB, depending on the DBMS (PostgreSQL 8 KB, InnoDB 16 KB, SQL Server 8 KB). Each page has a page ID. A table or index is made of many pages. If a row does not fit in a page, it spills into another page. WHAT IS FRAGMENTATION Related data is scattered across many non‐contiguous pages. LOW FRAGMENTATION (GOOD) HIGH FRAGMENTATION (BAD) Layout Pages 1, 2, 3, 4 physically next to each other Pages 1, 57, 12, 93: far apart on disk Result Sequential I/O More I/O, slower queries, more seeks TWO KINDS EXTERNAL INTERNAL What Free space exists, but scattered in small pieces Unused space inside an allocated page Effect A large contiguous block is not available Happens when page size is larger than the data stored Example Need 40 KB, largest contiguous free space is smaller 8 KB page holding 5 KB of data wastes 3 KB HOW IT HAPPENS Inserts. New rows land in the middle of pages (for indexes), causing page splits. Pages get scattered. Updates. A row grows and no longer fits in its page, so it is moved and leaves a hole.

Deletes. Removed rows leave free space inside pages. Over time many holes mean under‐utilised pages, and the space is not reused efficiently. PAGE SPLITS IN A CLUSTERED INDEX A B+ tree has leaves 10, 20, 30, 40 | 60, 70, 80, 90. Inserting 25, 35 and 45 into the middle of full pages splits them, creating new pages and more of them overall: frag‐ mentation increases. IMPACT More disk I/O, since data is scattered. Slower queries: range scans and joins suffer. More space used, as internal fragmentation wastes it. Lower throughput: more I/O means lower performance. HOW TO REDUCE IT Use sequential inserts (identity / auto‐increment keys). Avoid random inserts into clustered indexes. Random GUIDs cause high page splits. Use a fill factor : leave some free space in pages. Use an appropriate page size. Maintain regularly: rebuild or reorganise indexes, defragment tables (DBMS‐spe‐ cific). Partition large tables. MEMORY TRICK A bookshelf is a set of pages. To insert a book in the middle, you create a new shelf and move some books onto it. That is a page split , and it is what causes fragmenta‐ tion. R E M E M B E R . Fragmentation happens when data is not stored contiguously on disk, causing more I/O, slower queries and wasted space. Main causes: inserts, updates, deletes. Prevent with good design and regular maintenance.

PART IV Transactions and Concurrency ACID, isolation levels and their anomalies, optimistic and pessim‐ istic locking, and what @Transactional really does. ACID Transactions Isolation Levels Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking How @Transactional Works Internally

CHAPTER 14 ACID Transactions A transaction groups statements into one unit of work. ACID is the set of guarantees it gives. PROPERT Y MEANING MECHANISM (T YPIC‐ AL) Atomicity All or nothing Undo log, rollback Consistency The database moves from one valid state to another Constraints, triggers Isolation Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other Locks, MVCC Durability Once committed, changes are permanent Write-ahead log, fsync THE CLASSIC EXAMPLE A transfer debits one account and credits another. Atomicity means either both happen or neither. Consistency means total money is unchanged and constraints hold. Isolation means no one sees the debit without the credit. Durability means a crash right after commit does not lose the transfer. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; -- or ROLLBACK on any failure R E M E M B E R . Isolation is the only ACID property with levels: you trade consist‐ ency against concurrency. The next chapter is exactly that trade.

ISOLATION LEVELS CHAPTER 15 Isolation Levels Isolation is a property of database transactions that determines how and when changes made by one transaction become visible to other concurrent transactions. WHY IT MATTERS Multiple transactions may run concurrently. The isolation level controls the bal‐ ance between data consistency and concurrency. Higher isolation means more consistency but lower concurrency. WHAT CAN GO WRONG ANOMALY WHAT HAPPENS Dirty read T1 writes but has not committed; T2 reads that uncommitted data. If T1 rolls back, T2 read data that never existed Non-repeatable T1 reads a row; T2 updates it and commits; T1 reads again and gets a read different value Phantom read T1 reads a set of rows; T2 inserts a new matching row and commits; T1 reads again and sees an extra row THE FOUR LEVELS, LOWEST TO HIGHEST Read Uncommitted. Transactions can read data modified by others even if not committed. Allows dirty reads. Highest concurrency, lowest consistency. Read Committed. A transaction reads only committed data. Prevents dirty reads, allows non‐repeatable reads. Common default in Oracle, SQL Server and Postgr‐ eSQL. Repeatable Read. Rows read once cannot change during the transaction. Pre‐ vents dirty and non‐repeatable reads. May allow phantom reads, depending on the implementation. Default in MySQL InnoDB. Serializable. Transactions behave as if run one after another. Prevents all three anomalies. Maximum consistency, lowest concurrency, highest overhead.

COMPARISON LEVEL DIRT Y READ NON-REPEAT‐ ABLE READ PHANTOM READ NOTES Read Possible Possible Possible Lowest isolation, highest Uncommitted concurrency Read Prevented Possible Possible Common default Committed Repeatable Prevented Prevented Possible* *May be prevented in some Read DBMS (MySQL InnoDB) Serializable Prevented Prevented Prevented Highest isolation, lowest concurrency WORKED EXAMPLES Non-repeatable read (Read Committed). -- T1: SELECT salary --. -> 5000 -- T2: UPDATE salary = 6000; COMMIT; -- T1: SELECT salary --. -> 6000 (same query, different result) Phantom read (Repeatable Read). -- T1: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept = 'IT'; -- 10 rows -- T2: INSERT new IT employee; COMMIT; -- T1: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept = 'IT'; -- 11 rows (phantom) COMMON DEFAULTS DATABASE DEFAULT Oracle Read Committed SQL Server Read Committed PostgreSQL Read Committed MySQL (InnoDB) Repeatable Read CHOOSING A LEVEL Strong consistency, such as banking, means a higher level (Serializable). Higher performance means a lower level (Read Committed). Higher isolation costs more locking or versioning overhead. R E M E M B E R . Choose the isolation level by requirement, and be ready to say which anomaly each level allows.

OPTIMISTIC VS PESSIMISTIC LOCKING CHAPTER 16 Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking Concurrency-control mechanisms that prevent data inconsistency when multiple transactions try to update the same data. OPTIMISTIC PESSIMISTIC Assumption Conflicts are rare Conflicts are common Locking No lock during read Lock acquired immediately Mechanism Version number or timestamp Row or table locks, SELECT --. FOR UPDATE Conflict handling Detected at update/commit time Prevented before the update Throughput and High Lower scalability Deadlock risk None Possible Best for Read-heavy systems Write-heavy systems OPTIMISTIC FLOW Read data → Modify data → Check version → Version same? Update Otherwise retry or fail → Example with a version column: Initial record: id 1, balance 1000, version 1. User A and User B both read it. User A updates: UPDATE account SET balance = 900, version = 2 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 1; Success. 2. User B updates: UPDATE account SET balance = 800, version = 2 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 1; Fails, since the version is already 2. Conflict detected. PESSIMISTIC FLOW SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Acquire lock Modify data Commit or rollback → → → Release lock → Other transactions that need the same row must wait until the first commits.

Example: Transaction A runs SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE , the row is locked, it updates the balance and commits, and the lock is released. Transaction B issues the same statement, waits, then acquires the lock and proceeds. IN SPRING DATA JPA Optimistic: add a version field. @Entity public class Account { @Id private Long id; private Double balance; @Version private Long version; } -/ Generated: UPDATE --. WHERE id = ? AND version = ? -/ On mismatch: OptimisticLockException (Spring wraps it as ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException) Pessimistic: lock on read. @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) @Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.id = :id") Account findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id); -/ Generated: SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = ? FOR UPDATE WHEN TO USE WHICH OPTIMISTIC WHEN PESSIMISTIC WHEN Reads far outnumber writes Writes are frequent Probability of conflict is low Contention on the same data is high High scalability matters Data integrity is critical Web apps and microservices Deadlock handling is acceptable User profiles, product catalogue, CMS, blogs Banking, trading, inventory, ticket booking THE 30-SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare and uses a version field to detect concurrent updates at commit time. It scales better because no lock is held. Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are common and locks the data with SELECT FOR UPDATE , preventing other transactions from modifying it until the transaction completes. Use optimistic for read-heavy systems, and pessimistic when data consistency is critical and write contention is high. QUICK MEMORY TRICK Optimistic: "Trust first, verify later." Pessimistic: "Lock first, then work." R E M E M B E R . Optimistic: no lock, check version, update. Pessimistic: lock, up‐ date, commit, release.

HOW @TRANSACTIONAL WORKS INTERNALLY CHAPTER 17 How @Transactional Works Internally @Transactional is a declarative way to manage transactions. Spring achieves it with AOP proxies, transaction interceptors and a PlatformTransactionManager . KEY COMPONENTS COMPONENT ROLE @Transactional Declares the transactional boundary AOP proxy (JDK or CGLIB) Intercepts calls to the bean TransactionInterceptor PlatformTransactionManager TransactionSynchronizationManager Around advice that wraps the method Begins, commits and rolls back the transaction Binds resources (connection, session) to the current thread WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE METHOD IS CALLED Client AOP proxy TransactionInterceptor PlatformTransactionManager → → → Target method Commit or rollback Cleanup → → → 2. 3. 4. The client calls the method on a Spring bean. The call goes through the proxy (JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB). The proxy delegates to TransactionInterceptor (a MethodInterceptor ). The interceptor reads the transaction attributes (propagation, isolation, timeout, read‐ only) and calls PlatformTransactionManager.getTransaction() . A new transaction is created, or an existing one is joined, according to propagation. Re‐ sources (connection, session) are bound to the current thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager . The target method, your business logic, runs. On success the transaction commits . On an exception it rolls back according to the roll‐ back rules. Resources are unbound and cleaned up from the thread, and the result (or exception) re‐ turns to the caller. 5. 7. 8. CALL STACK, SIMPLIFIED Client -> Proxy (JDK / CGLIB) -> TransactionInterceptor (MethodInterceptor) -> PlatformTransactionManager (begin / commit / rollback) -> Target method (business logic) -> Database / resource

PROPAGATION BEHAVIOURS PROPAGATION WHAT IT DOES REQUIRED (default) Join an existing transaction, or create a new one if none REQUIRES_NEW Always create a new transaction (suspends the current one) SUPPORTS Join if one exists, otherwise run non-transactionally NOT_SUPPORTED Run non-transactionally MANDATORY Must run within an existing transaction NEVER Must not run within a transaction NESTED Nested transaction (savepoint), if supported If transfer() calls another @Transactional method with REQUIRES_NEW , that method runs in a separate transaction. ROLLBACK RULES By default RuntimeException and Error trigger a rollback. Checked exceptions do not. Cus‐ tomise with rollbackFor and noRollbackFor . @Transactional( rollbackFor = {IOException.class, CustomException.class}, noRollbackFor = {BusinessException.class} ) public void process() { --. } WHAT HAPPENS DURING COMMIT AND ROLLBACK COMMIT ROLLBACK beforeCommit() beforeCompletion() beforeCompletion() Actual rollback in the database Actual commit in the database afterCompletion(STATUS_ROLLED_BACK) afterCommit() afterCompletion(STATUS_COMMITTED) PITFALLS @Transactional works only on public methods called through the proxy. Self-invocation (a call within the same class) bypasses the proxy, so the annotation has no effect. Move the method to another bean. It works with DataSourceTransactionManager (JDBC) or JpaTransactionManager (JPA). In reactive apps, use the reactive transaction manager; thread‐bound resources do not apply. REMEMBER. @Transactional is Spring AOP plus a transaction manager. It creates a transaction boundary around your method and manages resources, with com‐ mit or rollback.

WHY REDIS IS SO FAST CHAPTER 21 Why Redis Is So Fast Redis is an in-memory data-structure server, optimised for speed at every layer. Eight reasons stack together. IN-MEMORY DATA STORE All data lives in RAM, which is orders of magnitude faster than disk. MEDIUM APPROXIMATE ACCESS TIME RAM ~100 nanoseconds SSD ~100 microseconds HDD ~10 milliseconds That is roughly 1000x between RAM and SSD, and far more against a spinning disk. SINGLE-THREADED EVENT LOOP Commands are executed by a single thread driven by an event loop on I/O multi‐ plexing ( epoll / kqueue ). No context switching, no lock contention, predictable performance, and it still handles thousands of connections. Since Redis 6, optional I/O threads can read and write sockets in parallel, but com‐ mand execution stays single‐threaded. EFFICIENT DATA STRUCTURES String, Hash, List, Set, Sorted Set, Bitmap, HyperLogLog, Geospatial: simple, highly optimised structures implemented in C, with O(1) time for most operations. OPTIMISED I/O MODEL OS‐level I/O multiplexing ( epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows) lets one thread serve many connections with high throughput and low latency. Non‐blocking I/O keeps the server busy with useful work, not waiting.

RESP PROTOCOL A lightweight, simple text protocol with minimal parsing overhead. It supports pipelining : sending several commands in one network round trip. Less data on the wire, fewer round trips, more throughput. ZERO-COPY AND EFFICIENT MEMORY MANAGEMENT Zero‐copy techniques such as sendfile and writev reduce copying between kernel and user space. Memory is managed by jemalloc , a memory allocator that favours performance and limits fragmentation. PERSISTENCE DONE ASYNCHRONOUSLY RDB snapshots and the AOF (append‐only file) are handled in the background (RDB via a forked child process; AOF fsync policy is configurable), so persistence does not block the main thread under normal operation. SMALL, OPTIMISED CODEBASE Written in ANSI C, portable and highly optimised. A small codebase is easy to audit, maintain and tune. SUMMARY In‐memory speed, single‐threaded event loop, efficient data structures, optimised I/ O, lightweight protocol, zero‐copy and efficient memory, async persistence, and an optimised codebase together make Redis extremely fast, predictable and efficient. R E M E M B E R . A single big or slow command (for example KEYS * on a large key‐ space) blocks everything. Redis is fast because the work per command is tiny, not because it does many things at once.

POSTGRESQL CONNECTION POOLING CHAPTER 22 PostgreSQL Connection Pooling Opening a database connection is expensive. A pool opens connections once and reuses them. WHY A CONNECTION IS EXPENSIVE STEP APPROXIMATE COST TCP handshake ~1 ms TLS negotiation ~5 ms DB authentication ~3 ms Session setup ~1 to 2 ms Total overhead ~10 ms+ Every request that opens its own connection pays this. At 1000 requests per second, that is 10 seconds of wasted time per second. In PostgreSQL, each connection also consumes a backend process on the database server. RECOMMENDED POOL SIZE A commonly cited formula (PostgreSQL): pool_size = (CPU cores x 2) + effective_spindle_count Example: a 4‐core machine with SSD gives a pool size of about 9 to 10, which is suffi‐ cient in most cases. More connections means more contention and less through- put. A small pool with a queue beats a huge pool. REAL IMPLEMENTATIONS TOOL T YPE NOTES HikariCP (Java / In-app Fastest Java pool, Spring Boot default; low latency, high Spring Boot) pool throughput, production proven pgBouncer Proxy Sits between the app and PostgreSQL; maps thousands of (PostgreSQL) pooler clients to few DB connections; transaction and session pooling; small memory footprint

TOOL T YPE NOTES pg-pool (Node.js) In-app pool Official PostgreSQL pool for Node; simple, lightweight, single process SQLAlchemy In-app Configurable pool_size , max_overflow ; timeouts and recycle (Python) pool support SPRING BOOT CONFIGURATION spring: datasource: hikari: maximum-pool-size: 10 minimum-idle: 5 connection-timeout: 3000 # fail fast, in ms max-lifetime: 1800000 idle-timeout: 600000 BEST PRACTICES Always use connection pooling. Size the pool from the formula (CPU x 2 + disks), not from the request rate. Never open and close a connection per request. Use transaction pooling (pgBouncer) for high concurrency. Set connection timeouts so failures are fast. Monitor pool metrics: active, idle, waiting. Do not exceed max_connections on the PostgreSQL server, summed across all ap‐ plication instances. COMMON USE CASES Web applications, microservices, APIs, batch jobs, reporting systems, ETL pipelines, real‐time analytics, serverless functions, legacy systems. R E M E M B E R . Reuse connections, reduce latency and maximise throughput. Pool smart, scale better.

DATABASE OPTIMIZATION CHAPTER 23 Database Optimization Build fast, scalable and cost-effective data systems. WHY OPTIMISE Faster queries, better resource use, lower latency, higher throughput, lower cost, scalability and reliability. Track key metrics : latency (p95/p99), QPS/TPS, throughput, CPU/ memory/IOPS, cache hit ratio, lock wait time, slow-query count. SYSTEM DESIGN VIEW Clients -> Load balancer -> App servers --> Cache layer (Redis / Memcached) --> Database cluster Primary (writes) Replicas (reads) --> Object storage (S3 / GCS) Monitoring and observability: metrics, logs, alerts Reads fan out to replicas and cache; writes go to the primary. SCHEMA AND MODELING BEST PRACTICES Use appropriate data types (the smallest that fits). Normalise when it helps, denormalise for performance when measured. Choose the right keys (primary, composite, surrogate). Avoid nullable columns in large tables. Use consistent naming conventions. INDEXING STRATEGIES Index columns used in WHERE , JOIN , ORDER BY , GROUP BY . Use composite indexes for multi-column filters. High cardinality before low cardinality in the key order. Avoid over-indexing, since indexes slow writes. Regularly review unused indexes. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at); -- composite CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cover ON orders(status, created_at, amount); -- covering -- Avoid: low-selectivity index CREATE INDEX idx_gender ON users(gender); QUERY OPTIMISATION DO AVOID Select only needed columns SELECT * on large tables Use LIMIT for large results Unbounded result sets

DO AVOID Use EXISTS instead of IN with subqueries (where it helps) Functions on indexed columns Filter early, join later Ignoring query plans Use proper data types Not analysing slow queries Analyse and profile queries -- Bad: function on the column defeats the index SELECT o.id, o.amount FROM orders o WHERE DATE(o.created_at) = '2024-05-01'; -- Good: a range the index can use SELECT o.id, o.amount FROM orders o WHERE o.created_at -= '2024-05-01' AND o.created_at CACHING STRATEGIES Cache what is read frequently, expensive to compute, or reference/static. Cache query results carefully. PATTERN HOW IT WORKS Cache-aside (lazy loading) App checks the cache; on a miss reads the DB and populates the cache Write-through Writes go to cache and DB together Write-behind Writes go to cache, flushed to the DB asynchronously Invalidation The hard part: expire or evict entries when data changes Read from cache → Hit? return data → Miss: read from DB → Populate cache SCALING STRATEGIES STRATEGY WHAT HOW Vertical (scale up) A bigger machine More CPU, RAM, IOPS; simple but has limits Horizontal (scale More machines Read replicas, sharding or partitioning, distribute the out) load Partitioning Split a big table Range, list or hash partitioning HIGH AVAILABILITY AND RELIABILITY Replication (primary and replicas), automatic failover, backups (full, incremental, pointin-time recovery), multi-AZ or multi-region, health checks and monitoring. Replication is usually asynchronous, so a replica can lag behind the primary; reads that must be fresh go to the primary. CONFIGURATION TUNING (POSTGRESQL EXAMPLE) AREA EXAMPLE SETTING Memory (buffer pool) shared_buffers about 25% of RAM Per-operation memory work_mem = 64 MB (per sort or hash, so mind concurrency) Maintenance maintenance_work_mem = 512 MB Planner cache estimate effective_cache_size about 75% of RAM Connections max_connections based on load, with pooling

DATABASE OPTIMIZATION AREA EXAMPLE SETTING Checkpoints checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9 SSD cost model random_page_cost = 1.1 MONITORING AND OBSERVABILITY Watch slow queries, lock waits, connections, CPU/memory, disk/IOPS and replication lag. Tools: Prometheus, Grafana, pg_stat_statements , performance_schema , CloudWatch. COMMON ANTI-PATTERNS SELECT * from large tables Missing indexes on joins and filters Too many indexes No LIMIT on large result sets Overuse of transactions Large unbounded text/blob columns in hot tables Ignoring query plans Not analysing slow queries PERFORMANCE CHECKLIST Schema designed for queries Indexes created and reviewed Queries optimised and tested Caching implemented where needed DB configuration tuned and documented Monitoring and alerts in place Capacity planning and load testing done QUICK COMMANDS EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123; ANALYZE orders; -- refresh planner statistics SHOW INDEXES FROM orders; -- MySQL -- MySQL slow queries SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Slow_queries'; GOLDEN RULE Measure, analyse, optimise, validate, monitor, repeat. Optimise the right queries: the 80/20 rule applies. Good design + good queries + good indexes + good infrastructure = high performance. R E M E M B E R . Do not tune what you have not measured.

CHAPTER 24 Change Data Capture (CDC) CDC is a design pattern that identifies and captures changes made to data in a source system and makes them available to downstream systems in real time or near real time. Source system → CDC Target system(s) → HOW CDC WORKS Detect change. Inserts, updates and deletes are detected in the source, via logs, triggers or timestamps. Capture. Changes are captured in the order they occur. Deliver. Changes are streamed or published to target systems. Consume. Downstream systems consume and apply the changes. CAPTURE METHODS METHOD HOW NOTES Transaction-log Read the database transaction log Low impact on the source, mining (MySQL binlog, PostgreSQL WAL, SQL Server CDC, Oracle redo logs) captures deletes, preserves order; the preferred method Triggers Database triggers write changes to a change table or log Simple, but adds write overhead on the source Timestamp / Query rows using a last-updated Easy, but misses hard deletes versioning timestamp or version number and relies on polling Application- The application publishes an event for Full control, but must be done in based each data change every code path (see the outbox pattern) BENEFITS Real‐time or near‐real‐time data sync. Minimal impact on the source system (log‐based). Improved data consistency. Enables event‐driven architectures.

CHANGE DATA CAPTURE (CDC) Supports analytics, reporting and microservices integration. COMMON USE CASES Real‐time analytics and reporting, data warehousing and ETL/ELT, data replication and synchronisation, event‐driven microservices, audit, monitoring and compli‐ ance, search synchronisation, cache updates. CHALLENGES Log growth and management, handling schema changes, ensuring data consist‐ ency and ordering, de‐duplication and idempotency, increased complexity in setup and monitoring. POPULAR TOOLS Debezium, AWS DMS (Database Migration Service), Oracle GoldenGate, StreamSets, Flink CDC, Kafka Connect (with CDC connectors). PIPELINE ARCHITECTURE PostgreSQL Write-ahead log CDC connector (Debezium) Event stream (Kafka) → → → Consumers → A change is made in the source database ( INSERT orders , UPDATE products ). The change is recorded in the transaction log (the WAL). The CDC connector reads changes from the log, continuously. Changes are converted into events and published to topics ( orders_topic , customers_topic , products_topic ). Consumers process the events in real time: Elasticsearch (search), Redis (cache), a data warehouse (analytics), microservices (events). CONSUMER-SIDE RULES Delivery is typically at least once , so consumers must be idempotent. Ordering is guaranteed per partition (usually per key), not globally. Plan for schema evolution and for initial snapshots when onboarding a new table. R E M E M B E R . CDC enables systems to react to data changes as they happen, powering real‐time integrations, analytics and modern data architectures.

Always validate in production. COMMON INTERVIEW QUESTIONS, WITH THE SHORT ANSWER What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP? DELETE removes selected rows (DML, rollback‐able, slower). TRUNCATE removes all rows and keeps the table (DDL, fast). DROP removes the table itself. What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. What is an index and how does it work? A sorted auxiliary structure (usually a B+ tree) mapping column values to row locations, turning an O(N) scan into an O(log N) lookup, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Explain ACID with an example. A bank transfer: both the debit and credit happen or neither (atomic); constraints hold (consistent); no one sees half the transfer (isol‐ ated); a committed transfer survives a crash (durable). What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF, 3NF. Organising data to reduce redund‐ ancy and anomalies. 1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependency on a composite key, 3NF no transitive dependency. How would you optimise a slow SQL query? Run EXPLAIN , look for full scans, add or fix indexes, select only needed columns, avoid functions on indexed columns, re‐ fresh statistics, add LIMIT , consider caching or denormalisation.

RAPID REVISION SQL vs NoSQL: when to use which? SQL for structured data, joins and strong con‐ sistency. NoSQL for flexible schema, horizontal scale or specialised access patterns (cache, graph, time series). Often both. Explain joins with examples. Inner returns matching rows; left keeps all left rows with NULLs on no match; right the mirror; full keeps all; cross is every combina‐ tion. FIVE ANSWERS WORTH MEMORISING Clustered versus non-clustered: data is physically in index order versus a sep‐ arate structure with pointers. One clustered per table. Optimistic versus pessimistic: version check at commit versus lock up front. Trust first, verify later versus lock first, then work. Isolation anomalies: dirty read (uncommitted), non‐repeatable read (row changed), phantom read (new row appears). Why a query ignores an index: function on the column, type mismatch, lead‐ ing wildcard, low selectivity, OR across columns, stale statistics, composite‐in‐ dex order. SQL execution order: FROM , JOIN , WHERE , GROUP BY , HAVING , SELECT , ORDER BY , LIMIT . R E M E M B E R . Understand the trade‐offs, measure before you optimise, and choose the database that fits the workload. Measure first. Then index, cache and scale. DATABASE INTERVIEW NOTES
